# Modern Web Guidance (Source) This repo is the source repository for [GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance) and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents. [**Modern Web Guidance**](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) and [GOVERNANCE.md](./GOVERNANCE.md) for how we work on the project and orientation of the codebase. --- *Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.* [Documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) · [Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/) · [Source Code](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src) · [Report an Issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues) ## Quickstart ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install ``` This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See [Alternative Installation Methods](#-alternative-installation-methods) below. #### Try it out (without installing) ```shell # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer" # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . ``` ## Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. **Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: * **Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. * **Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. ## What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. ### Core Disciplines

🎨 User Experience

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).

📐 CSS Layout

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

⚡ Performance

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).

📝 Forms & UI

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

♿ Accessibility

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

🤖 Built-in AI

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
_View an example:_ [the `navigation-drawer` guide](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-components/navigation-drawer.md). #### The full list

**[optimize-script-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/optimize-script-priority.md)**: Optimize the loading priority of scripts by boosting critical asynchronous scripts and deprioritizing non-essential or late-body scripts to improve sequencing and reduce delays. - **[out-of-order-html-streaming](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/out-of-order-html-streaming.md)**: Declaratively update a page with content streamed later into the same HTML document or via imperative JavaScript APIs. - - **[agentic-forms](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/webmcp/agentic-forms.md)**: Expose client-side functionality as tools to AI agents by annotating standard HTML forms with WebMCP attributes. - **[agentic-javascript-tools](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/webmcp/agentic-javascript-tools.md)**: Programmatically register client-side JavaScript functions as tools for AI agents using the WebMCP Imperative API. - **[webmcp](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/webmcp/webmcp.md)**: Use this guide to implement WebMCP in browser applications, exposing client-side functionality as tools to AI agents via declarative or imperative APIs.
### Safe Adoption of Modern Features * **Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks**: We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles. * **Gotchas & Quirks**: We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for `fetchLater()` or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors. * **Baseline-Aware Integration**: We leverage real-time compatibility data from the **Baseline** project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support. * **Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates**: Guides covering experimental **Origin Trial** APIs or **volatile features** (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via `search`, but are gated on `retrieve` so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent. ### Project Configuration (`.mwgrc`) Configure Origin Trial and volatile feature opt-ins for a repository with an optional `.mwgrc` JSON file in your project root (or `~/.mwgrc` as a user-level fallback), which you can commit to share across your team: | CLI Command | `.mwgrc` Key | Effect | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-origin-trials` | `"allowOriginTrials": true` | Unlocks guides for experimental Origin Trial APIs. | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-volatile-features` | `"allowVolatileFeatures": true` | Unlocks guides for volatile single-engine features. | ## How It Works 1. **Activation**: The coding agent activates the `modern-web-guidance` skill because of a relevant task. The agent is instructed to use the `modern-web-guidance` CLI for web platform queries. 2. **Local Semantic Search**: The agent runs `modern-web-guidance search ""`. The tool matches the query to the best guide using an offline, zero-dependency embedding model and BM25 search engine (no network calls, no API keys). 3. **Guide Fetch**: The agent retrieves the guide via `modern-web-guidance retrieve `, inserting targeted code patterns, gotchas, and fallbacks directly into its context window. > [!TIP] > Note: We use `npx` to ensure the content doesn't go stale, but the CLI works offline, completely private and local. > The npm package is self-contained, with no extra dependencies to ensure both low-latency and supply-chain security. ## Alternative Installation Methods
Vercel Skills CLI (aka npx skills) ```shell npx skills add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
GitHub CLI ```shell gh skill install GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
Google Antigravity ```shell agy plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
GitHub Copilot CLI ```shell /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome ```
Claude Code Plugin ```shell /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome /plugin # Select GoogleChrome marketplace, press enter, enable AutoUpdate /reload-plugins ```
Grok Build CLI ```shell grok plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance --trust ```
Kimi Code ```shell /plugins install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
OpenAI Codex ```shell codex plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance codex plugin add modern-web-guidance@googlechrome ```
## Updating If you installed the skill using `npx modern-web-guidance@latest install`, you can update with: `npx modern-web-guidance@latest update`.
Claude Code (if installed via claude-plugins-official) Anthropic stopped updating third-party plugins in their built-in `claude-plugins-official` marketplace on Oct 12, stranding installs at `v0.0.194` ([details](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues/3533)). Switch to the `googlechrome` marketplace to get updates: ```shell /plugin uninstall modern-web-guidance@claude-plugins-official /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome /plugin # Select GoogleChrome marketplace, press enter, enable AutoUpdate /reload-plugins ```
Otherwise, consult your agent's documentation for updating plugins and skills. ## Evals to prove this works well We developed a robust eval harness to ensure that the content is **empirically proven and continuously calibrated** so AI agents write better code. We run automated evaluations using a closed-loop validation pipeline: ``` [ Expert-authored guidance and demo ] │ ▼ [ Target generation ] ──> Tasks on real webapps, Golden solutions, Playwright graders │ ▼ [ Calibration loop ] ───> Runs Grader on Golden Solutions (Must Pass 100%) │ Runs Grader on Unmodified Base App (Must Fail 100%) ▼ [ E2E agent evals ] ────> Runs coding agents in guided vs. unguided modes Compares pass rates and accessibility w/ and w/o the skill ``` 1. **Simulated Developer Tasks**: We define realistic developer prompts against full base applications (`daily-grind`, `devtools-times`) that mimic real-world requests (e.g., "make my images load faster"). Prompts avoid naming APIs or features, testing whether the agent can naturally discover and apply the right guides. 2. **Static & Browser-Based Checks**: Playwright graders verify that each implementation requirement was followed—checking source patterns, computed styles, runtime DOM behaviors, and accessibility states. 3. **Self-Healing Calibration**: Graders are calibrated against multi-agent (Claude/Codex/AGY) golden solutions (100% pass target) and an unmodified baseline application (0% pass target). 4. **E2E Testing**: We measure coding agent performance on real tasks with and without guidance. The _opportunity_ (100% - unguided pass rate) and _uplift_ (guided - unguided pass rate) are key: if models already succeed without guidance, we prune redundant advice; where agents struggle, we refine guides to maximize uplift. ### Recent eval results snapshot Explore full per-agent and per-guide breakdowns on the **[Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/)**. | Date | Agent + Model | Tasks / Checks | Unguided → Guided (Uplift) | | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | | Nov 8 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 214 / 1673 | 58% → 94% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 8 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 215 / 1795 | 54% → 82% (**+28pp**) | | Nov 8 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 215 / 1801 | 57% → 88% (**+31pp**) | | Nov 6 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 212 / 1773 | 53% → 86% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 6 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 212 / 1773 | 56% → 90% (**+34pp**) | | Nov 6 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 212 / 1722 | 60% → 96% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 4 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 209 / 1743 | 52% → 85% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 4 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 209 / 1743 | 57% → 90% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 4 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 207 / 1722 | 60% → 96% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 2 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 205 / 1729 | 55% → 82% (**+27pp**) | ## Available Skill Packs You can customize which skill packs are installed using the `--choose` flag: ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install --choose ``` * **`modern-web-guidance`** (~205 tokens): Comprehensive guidance on modern browser APIs, layouts, and performance. * **`chrome-extensions`** (~175 tokens): Guidance on Manifest V3, background workers, extension APIs, and Chrome Web Store publishing. ## Telemetry & Privacy Google collects anonymous usage information to improve the tool's reliability, relevance, and performance. Collected information includes installation counts, the calling agent name, guide retrieval IDs, and CLI tool search queries generated by the agent (e.g. "dark mode scrollbar color-scheme"). Raw user prompts are not collected. You can inspect what is collected in [modern-web.ts](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/main/src/cli/modern-web.ts). > [!TIP] > **To Opt-Out:** set the `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` env variable in your shell profile (e.g., `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`): > ```bash > export DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 > ``` Google handles this data in accordance with the [Google Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy). ## Contributors Found a bug, outdated pattern, or missing web platform feature? [Open an issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues) or see [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) in the [source repository (`GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src`)](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src). Huge thanks to everyone who has contributed! ## License Unless otherwise noted: * Software code in this project is licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/main/LICENSE). * Documentation and guide content under `guides/` are licensed under [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY 4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). repositories.name: open-code-review
repositories.description: Secure, fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.
repositories.readme:
OpenCodeReview

English | 简体中文 | 日本語 | 한국어 | Русский

--- ## What is Open Code Review? Open Code Review is an AI-powered code review CLI tool. It originated as Alibaba Group's internal official AI code review assistant — over the past two years, it has served tens of thousands of developers and identified millions of code defects. After thorough validation at massive scale, we incubated it into an open source project for the community. Simply configure a model endpoint to get started. It reads Git diffs, sends changed files to a configurable LLM via an agent with tool-use capabilities, and generates structured review comments with line-level precision. The agent can read full file contents, search the codebase, inspect other changed files for context, and produce deep reviews — not just surface-level diff feedback. Beyond diff review, `ocr scan` reviews entire files for auditing unfamiliar codebases or directories that have no meaningful diff. Visit the [official website](https://open-codereview.ai) for more details. ![Highlights](imgs/highlights-en.png) ## Benchmark > Compared to general-purpose agents (Claude Code), Open Code Review achieves significantly higher **Precision** and **F1** with the same underlying model, while consuming only **~1/9 of the tokens** and completing reviews faster. Note that its Recall is lower than general-purpose agents — a deliberate trade-off favoring precision over noise. A real-world code review benchmark built from **50** popular open-source repositories, **200** real Pull Requests, and **10** programming languages — cross-validated by 80+ senior engineers (**1,505** annotated ground-truth issues). Explore the AACR-Bench dataset on Hugging Face. | Metric | What it measures | Why it matters | |--------|-----------------|----------------| | **F1** | Harmonic mean of precision and recall | Best single number for overall review quality | | **Precision** | Proportion of reported issues that are real defects | Higher = fewer false alarms to triage | | **Recall** | Proportion of real defects that are found | Higher = fewer issues slip through review | | **Avg Time** | Wall-clock time per review | Matters for CI pipeline latency | | **Avg Token** | Total tokens consumed per review | Directly impacts API cost | ![Benchmark](imgs/benchmark-en.png) ## Why Open Code Review? ### The Problem with General-Purpose Agents If you've used general-purpose agents like Claude Code with Skills for code review, you've likely encountered these pain points: - **Incomplete coverage** — On larger changesets, agents tend to "cut corners," selectively reviewing only some files and missing others. - **Position drift** — Reported issues frequently don't match the actual code location, with line numbers or file references drifting off target. - **Unstable quality** — Natural-language-driven Skills are hard to debug, and review quality fluctuates significantly with minor prompt variations. The root cause: a purely language-driven architecture lacks hard constraints on the review process. ### Core Design: Deterministic Engineering × Agent Hybrid Open Code Review's core philosophy is to combine deterministic engineering with an agent, each handling what it does best. **Deterministic Engineering — Hard Constraints** For review steps that *must not go wrong*, engineering logic — not the language model — guarantees correctness: - **Precise file selection** — Determines exactly which files need review and which should be filtered, ensuring no important change is missed. - **Smart file bundling** — Groups related files into a single review unit (e.g., `message_en.properties` and `message_zh.properties` are bundled together). Each bundle runs as a sub-agent with isolated context — a divide-and-conquer strategy that stays stable on very large changesets and naturally supports concurrent review. - **Fine-grained rule matching** — Matches review rules to each file's characteristics, keeping the model's attention sharply focused and eliminating information noise at the source. Compared to purely language-driven rule guidance, template-engine-based rule matching is more stable and predictable. - **External positioning and reflection modules** — Independent comment-positioning and comment-reflection modules systematically improve both the location accuracy and content accuracy of AI feedback. **Agent — Dynamic Decision-Making** The agent's strengths are concentrated where they matter most — dynamic decisions and dynamic context retrieval: - **Scenario-tuned prompts** — Prompt templates deeply optimized for code review, improving effectiveness while reducing token consumption. - **Scenario-tuned toolset** — Distilled from deep analysis of tool-call traces in large-scale production data — including call frequency distributions, per-tool repetition rates, and the impact of new tools on the overall call chain — resulting in a purpose-built toolset that is more stable and predictable for code review than a generic agent toolkit. ## How to Use ### Prerequisites - **Git >= 2.41** — Open Code Review relies on Git for diff generation, code search, and repository operations. ### CLI #### Install ```bash npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review ``` After installation, the `ocr` command is available globally. For other installation methods (install script, GitHub Release binary, from source), see [Installation](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/installation). #### Quick Start **1. Configure LLM** You must configure an LLM before reviewing code, unless you use [Delegation Mode](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/delegate). - **OCR calls the model:** `ocr review`, the `/open-code-review:review` command, and the `open-code-review` skill use OCR's own provider configuration, not your Claude Code Team/Pro subscription login. Authentication requirements depend on the provider; see [Configuration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration). - **The host agent calls the model:** the `/open-code-review:delegate-review` command and the `open-code-review-delegate` skill use the host agent's configured model and authentication. No separate LLM configuration or credentials are needed in OCR. See the [Claude Code install steps](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#claude-code). ```bash ocr config provider # Select a built-in provider or add a custom one ocr config model # Pick a model for the active provider ``` ![Provider setup](imgs/providers.jpg) The interactive UI guides you through provider selection, API key entry, and model configuration, then automatically tests connectivity. For CLI setup, environment variables, custom providers, and other advanced configuration, see [Configuration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration). **2. Review** ```bash cd your-project # Workspace mode — review all staged, unstaged, and untracked changes ocr review # Branch range — reviews feature-branch's changes since it diverged from main (merge-base mode) ocr review --from main --to feature-branch # Single commit ocr review --commit abc123 # Resume an interrupted range or commit review ocr session list ocr review --from main --to feature-branch --resume # Full-file scan — review whole files instead of a diff (no git history needed) ocr scan # scan the entire repository ocr scan --path internal/agent # scan a directory or specific files ocr scan --resume # resume an interrupted full-file scan # Save results to a file (recommended for AI host agents) ocr review --format json --output result.json # Delegation mode — let your AI coding agent perform the review itself # OCR handles file selection and rule resolution; no LLM configuration needed ocr delegate preview ocr delegate rule src/main.go src/handler.go ``` ## Documentation Full documentation lives at **[open-codereview.ai/docs](https://open-codereview.ai/docs)**: - [Quickstart](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/quickstart) — install and run your first review - [Installation](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/installation) — all platforms and package managers - [CLI Reference](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/cli-reference) — every command and flag - [Review Rules](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/review-rules) — customize review rules with path filtering and targeting - [Configuration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration) — config keys and environment variables - [MCP Server](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/mcp) — extend the review agent with external tools - Coding Agent Integrations — choose the platform you use - [Claude Code](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#claude-code) — install a plugin with review slash commands - [Codex](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#codex) — install a plugin with callable review skills - [Cursor](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#cursor) — install a plugin with portable review skills - [Kimi Code](plugins/open-code-review/README.md#kimi-code) — install a plugin with review slash commands and skills - [OpenCode](plugins/open-code-review/opencode/README.md) — install native review tools and slash commands - [QCA Forward](plugins/open-code-review/qca/README.md) — run delegation mode with the QCA host model and a ready-to-publish template - [Skill-compatible agents](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/agent-skill) — install the portable agent skill - Review Execution Modes — after integration, choose which LLM performs the review - [Default (OCR-managed)](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/configuration) — OCR runs the review using its configured LLM - [Delegation Mode](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/delegate) — your coding agent runs the review using its own LLM; no OCR API key required - [CI/CD Integration](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/cicd) — GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, GitFlic CI, and Gerrit integration - [Session Viewer](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/viewer) — browse and replay review sessions in browser, mark comments as fixed or ignored and hide them while you work through the findings - [Telemetry](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/telemetry) — OpenTelemetry integration for observability - [FAQ](https://open-codereview.ai/docs/faq) — common questions and troubleshooting ## Contributing This project exists thanks to all the people who contribute. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup, coding guidelines, and how to submit pull requests. ## License [Apache-2.0](LICENSE) — Copyright 2026 Alibaba

repositories.description: Chrome DevTools for coding agents
repositories.readme:
# Chrome DevTools for agents

[![npm chrome-devtools-mcp package](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/chrome-devtools-mcp.svg)](https://npmjs.org/package/chrome-devtools-mcp)

Chrome DevTools for agents (`chrome-devtools-mcp`) lets your coding agent (such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor or Copilot)
control and inspect a live Chrome browser. It is available as a
Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server and as a [CLI][cli]. Both give your AI
coding assistant access to the full power of Chrome DevTools for reliable
automation, in-depth debugging, and performance analysis.

[Tool reference][tool-reference] | [CLI][cli] | [Skills][skills] | [Changelog][changelog] | [Contributing][contributing] | [Troubleshooting][troubleshooting] | [Design Principles][design-principles]

## Key features

- **Get performance insights**: Uses [Chrome
  DevTools](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/devtools-frontend) to record
  traces and extract actionable performance insights.
- **Advanced browser debugging**: Analyze network requests, take screenshots and
  check browser console messages (with source-mapped stack traces).
- **Reliable automation**. Uses
  [puppeteer](https://github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer) to automate actions in
  Chrome and automatically wait for action results.

## Disclaimers

`chrome-devtools-mcp` exposes content of the browser instance to the MCP clients
allowing them to inspect, debug, and modify any data in the browser or DevTools.
Avoid sharing sensitive or personal information that you don't want to share with
MCP clients.

`chrome-devtools-mcp` officially supports Google Chrome and [Chrome for Testing](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-for-testing/) only.
Other Chromium-based browsers may work, but this is not guaranteed, and you may encounter unexpected behavior. Use at your own discretion.
We are committed to providing fixes and support for the latest version of [Extended Stable Chrome](https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule).

Performance tools may send trace URLs to the Google CrUX API to fetch real-user
experience data. This helps provide a holistic performance picture by
presenting field data alongside lab data. This data is collected by the [Chrome
User Experience Report (CrUX)](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux). To disable
this, run with the `--no-performance-crux` flag.

## **Usage statistics**

Google collects usage statistics (such as tool invocation success rates, latency, and environment information) to improve the reliability and performance of Chrome DevTools MCP.

Data collection is **enabled by default**. You can opt-out by passing the `--no-usage-statistics` flag when starting the server:

```json
"args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest", "--no-usage-statistics"]
```

Google handles this data in accordance with the [Google Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy).

Google's collection of usage statistics for Chrome DevTools MCP is independent from the Chrome browser's usage statistics. Opting out of Chrome metrics does not automatically opt you out of this tool, and vice-versa.

Collection is disabled if `CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_USAGE_STATISTICS` or `CI` env variables are set.

## Update checks

By default, the server periodically checks the npm registry for updates and logs a notification when a newer version is available.
You can disable these update checks by setting the `CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_UPDATE_CHECKS` environment variable.

## Requirements

- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) [LTS](https://github.com/nodejs/Release#release-schedule) version.
- [Chrome](https://www.google.com/chrome/) current stable version or newer.
- [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/)

## Getting started

Add the following config to your MCP client:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> Using `chrome-devtools-mcp@latest` ensures that your MCP client will always use the latest version of the Chrome DevTools MCP server.

### MCP Client configuration

For setup instructions specific to your editor or agent (e.g. Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code), please see our [Client Configurations Guide][client-configurations-guide].

### Your first prompt

Enter the following prompt in your MCP Client to check if everything is working:

```
Check the performance of https://developers.chrome.com
```

Your MCP client should open the browser and record a performance trace.

> [!NOTE]
> The MCP server will start the browser automatically once the MCP client uses a tool that requires a running browser instance. Connecting to the Chrome DevTools MCP server on its own will not automatically start the browser.

## CLI

The package also includes the `chrome-devtools` CLI. Use it to control the browser from your terminal without MCP:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
chrome-devtools navigate_page 1 --url "https://developers.chrome.com"
chrome-devtools take_screenshot 1 --filePath screenshot.png
chrome-devtools stop
```

See the [CLI guide][cli] for all commands and options.

## Skills

The package includes [skills](./skills) that teach your agent how to use Chrome DevTools:

| Skill                                                     | Use it to                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| [`chrome-devtools`](./skills/chrome-devtools)             | Debug and automate pages with the MCP tools.    |
| [`chrome-devtools-cli`](./skills/chrome-devtools-cli)     | Run the CLI and write shell scripts with it.    |
| [`a11y-debugging`](./skills/a11y-debugging)               | Audit and fix accessibility issues.             |
| [`cookie-debugging`](./skills/cookie-debugging)           | Debug cookies, sessions, and authentication.    |
| [`debug-optimize-lcp`](./skills/debug-optimize-lcp)       | Debug and improve Largest Contentful Paint.     |
| [`memory-leak-debugging`](./skills/memory-leak-debugging) | Find and fix memory leaks.                      |
| [`troubleshooting`](./skills/troubleshooting)             | Fix connection problems between MCP and Chrome. |

### Install skills as a plugin

A plugin installs the MCP server and all skills, including the CLI skill:

- **Claude Code:** Run `/plugin marketplace add ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`, then `/plugin install chrome-devtools-mcp@chrome-devtools-plugins`.
- **Copilot / VS Code:** Run **Chat: Install Plugin From Source** and enter `ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`.
- **Gemini CLI:** Run `gemini extensions install --auto-update https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`.

See the [Client Configurations Guide][client-configurations-guide] for more information.

### Install skills manually

If your agent does not support plugins, copy the skill folders into the skills directory of your agent. The npm package contains the skills:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
# Example for Claude Code. Use the skills directory of your agent.
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The `chrome-devtools-cli` skill requires the CLI. Install the package globally before you use the skill.

### Keep skills up to date

Skills describe the tools of a specific version. Update the skills each time you update the MCP server or the CLI. Outdated skills can tell your agent to use tools or parameters that changed.

- **Plugins:** Use the update command of the plugin manager of your agent. The Gemini CLI command above enables automatic updates with `--auto-update`.
- **Manual installs:** Update the package, then copy the skill folders again:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/
```

## Tools

If you run into any issues, checkout our [troubleshooting guide][troubleshooting].
See the full [Tool Reference][tool-reference] for a complete list of all supported MCP capabilities.

## Configuration

Find the complete list of server parameters (e.g., `--headless`, `--isolated`, `--slim`) and how to configure WebSocket connections in the [Configuration Guide][configuration-guide].

For basic browser tasks only, the `--slim` flag exposes a reduced set of tools. See the [Slim tool reference][slim-tool-reference].

## Advanced Usage

For advanced features such as handling concurrent sessions, persistent user data directories, using a custom or non-standard browser path (`--executablePath`), connecting to a running Chrome instance instead of starting a new one, or debugging on Android, see our [Advanced Usage Guide][advanced-usage-guide].

## Integrating as a browser subagent

If you are developing agentic tooling and want to provide an integrated browser subagent as part of your product, we recommend building on top of Chrome DevTools for agents.

For a reference implementation, see the [Gemini CLI browser agent documentation](https://geminicli.com/docs/core/subagents/#browser-agent).

repositories.description: OpenAI's Codex Security CLI and TypeScript SDK for finding, validating, and fixing security vulnerabilities. npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@openai/codex-security
repositories.readme:
# Codex Security

Codex Security helps you find, investigate, and fix vulnerabilities in your code.
Use its security workflows in Codex, or automate them with the
`@openai/codex-security` CLI and TypeScript SDK.

- **In Codex:** [choose a security workflow](docs/agent-workflows.md).
- **In a terminal:** [install the CLI and scan your repository](#quick-start).
- **In automation:** use the [TypeScript SDK](#typescript-sdk) or
  [GitHub Action](#github-actions).

## Features

- Scan repositories, selected paths, or Git changes. Deep scans repeat Standard scans and return their deduplicated findings.
- Validate candidate findings, generate patches, and verify existing fixes.
- Draft `SECURITY.md` policies and save threat models for later review.
- Browse saved scans and findings, identify duplicates, assess severity against
  your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history.
- Preview third-party scanner findings, save them locally, or publish supported reports to Codex Security Cloud. [Scanner import guides](docs/scanner-imports/README.md).
- Track findings in Linear, Jira, or GitHub, publish completed scans, or export SARIF, JSON, and CSV. [Integration workflows](docs/plugin-connectors.md).
- Automate scans across repositories or project components, including in CI and
  containers.

## Use in Codex

Open your repository in a Codex session with the Codex Security plugin enabled,
then ask:

> Run a Codex Security scan on this repository, focusing on authentication and
> authorization. Return the saved report, source evidence, and coverage limits.

A completed scan saves a report and findings. Read the report for source
evidence and exclusions, then request a patch or ask Codex to verify an
existing fix. See the [agent workflow guide](docs/agent-workflows.md) for setup,
task selection, and recovery.

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+.
Python 3.10 also requires `tomli`.

Install the CLI globally and sign in:

```bash
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
```

Run your first scan from the repository directory:

```bash
cs scan .
```

When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the **REPORT** path in the
terminal. Run `cs scans show` from the same repository to find its latest
completed scan again. See [scan scope and follow-up work](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#understand-scan-scope-and-follow-up-work)
for how to interpret exclusions in the report.

`cs` and `codex-security` run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with
another command, use `codex-security`. To skip the global install, or if npm
reports an `EEXIST` conflict, use `npx @openai/codex-security` in place of
`cs` for both login and scanning.

For CI, set `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `CODEX_API_KEY` in the scan process's environment.
For a headless machine, see [device or SSH login](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#authentication).

### Scan options

Choose a scope and scan mode:

```bash
# Scan selected paths.
cs scan . --path src --path tests

# Scan committed changes from a base revision to HEAD.
cs scan . --diff origin/main

# Run a deep scan of the repository.
cs scan . --mode deep
```

Use `cs scan . --max-time 15` for an advisory 15-minute Standard investigation
allowance. See [investigation time](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#set-investigation-time)
for timing semantics and Deep Scan limits.

Use `cs --help` to browse commands, or `cs scan --help`
for scan options, cost limits, and patching after a scan.

For an application spread across repositories, see
[review one system across repositories](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#review-one-system-across-repositories).
Use [bulk scans](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#bulk-scans) for independent repository
reviews in one resumable campaign.

Scans use existing root and component `SECURITY.md` guidance. To write or
revise it, see [Generate SECURITY.md](#generate-securitymd).

Some cybersecurity requests and protected findings require
[Trusted Access for Cyber](https://chatgpt.com/cyber). For accounts with Daybreak
access, see [Daybreak opt-in](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#daybreak-opt-in) for the
Codex toggle and [Cyber access programs](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#select-a-cyber-access-program)
to select a program explicitly.

## TypeScript SDK

Install the package locally in your TypeScript project:

```bash
npm install @openai/codex-security
```

Then import it:

```ts
import { CodexSecurity } from "@openai/codex-security";

const security = new CodexSecurity();

try {
  const result = await security.run("/path/to/repository");
  console.log(result.reportPath);
} finally {
  await security.close();
}
```

The [SDK guide](sdk/typescript/docs/sdk.md) includes deep-scan configuration,
validation, severity classification, owner suggestions, and result handling.

Linked Git worktrees share scan history and saved findings when they use the same
Codex Security state directory. Keep `CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR` stable to retain
that shared history and sign-in scope. See the [scan history guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#scan-history-and-reruns).

## Read existing Cloud findings

When Codex Security Cloud is available to your account, the Security plugin's
`$cloud-findings` skill can read findings, reports, recorded assignment and
verification, and scan status in Codex desktop or the Codex CLI. Cloud is an
optional connection; local scans work without it.

See [Cloud connection setup and CLI reads](sdk/typescript/docs/sdk.md#read-existing-cloud-findings)
for authentication requirements and a read-only example.

## Generate SECURITY.md

Use `policy` to draft a new `SECURITY.md` or update an existing one. Use `--path`
to select a component:

```bash
cs policy .
cs policy . --path services/api --knowledge-base architecture.md
```

The command saves its draft outside the repository and leaves existing files
unchanged. Review the diff and notes, edit the draft, then copy only `SECURITY.md`
to the displayed **Policy target**. Keep the saved architecture and threat-model
documents outside the repository.

Scans already use root and component `SECURITY.md` files. Keep your current policy
if it needs no changes. When updating it, preserve its vulnerability-reporting
instructions. If the command says the policy is already up to date, no copy is
needed.

Files at `.github/SECURITY.md` or `docs/SECURITY.md` often contain reporting
instructions. Preserve them when drafting a policy; those locations do not
automatically provide repository-wide scan guidance. See the
[policy guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#generate-a-security-policy) for policy
locations, unanswered questions, saved artifacts, and SDK usage.

## Save and export threat models

Scans and policy generation save threat models with their results. Export a saved
model without starting another analysis:

```bash
cs export --scan SCAN_ID --artifact threat-model --output threatmodel.md
```

Omit `--scan` to use the current repository's latest completed scan. The
[export guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#exports-and-ci) also covers findings,
SARIF output for CI, and the offline TypeScript API. For ServiceNow Application
Vulnerability Response, see [Export findings for ServiceNow](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#export-findings-for-servicenow).

## GitHub Actions

To run a weekly repository scan on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu:

1. Add an OpenAI API key as the repository secret `CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY`.
2. Copy the [weekly workflow](github-action/examples/repository.yml) to
   `.github/workflows/codex-security.yml`. Replace `REPLACE_WITH_REVIEWED_COMMIT`
   with the reviewed distribution commit SHA from an Action release.
3. To try the workflow before the next scheduled run, open **Actions → Codex
   Security repository → Run workflow**.

The example uses an estimated $5 limit per scan and reports findings without
failing the job. Requests in progress can exceed the limit. For a severity
threshold, pull request checks, or runner requirements, see the
[Action guide](github-action/README.md). For eligible accounts, see
[Daybreak access](github-action/README.md#daybreak-access-and-refusals).

## Containerized bulk scans

Scan a list of repositories with the included Docker Compose configuration,
which keeps results and authentication between runs. See the
[container quick start](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#containerized-bulk-scans).
The [workflow runner](docker/README.md#workflow-runner) runs individual CLI stages
in containers and can connect to a separately deployed findings service.

## Findings storage and deduplication

The [findings guide](sdk/typescript/docs/findings-service.md) covers local
storage, deduplication, and compatibility with independently operated endpoints
through `publish scan --to custom` and explicit `--findings-url`. The local
`serve` command and browser dashboard have been removed; existing databases and
scan artifacts remain available.

## Other providers

Scans support OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference. Bedrock uses
AWS credentials and does not require a separate OpenAI login. See
[Bedrock setup](docs/bedrock.md) for AWS profiles, regions, and model access.

For OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference, set the provider's API key and choose a supported
model. See [provider configuration](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#native-command-authentication-and-other-providers)
for examples.

## Documentation

- [Online documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/security/cli)
- [Agent workflows and recovery](docs/agent-workflows.md)
- [CLI reference](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md)
- [Imported finding identity and evidence](docs/scanner-imports/schema-guide.md)
- [Project configuration](docs/project-configuration.md)
- [Examples](examples/README.md)

To report a vulnerability privately, follow the [security policy](SECURITY.md).

repositories.name: univer
repositories.description: Build your own AI office with Univer Office SDK. Bring editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing into your product for people and AI agents. Built on an extensible open-source core.
repositories.readme:
Build your own AI office with Univer Office SDK.

Start with open-source Sheets and Docs, then connect your own application or agent.

🚀 Quick start · 📚 Documentation · ⚖️ Feature comparison · 🌐 Website · 🎮 Showcase · 🔧 API Reference · 📝 Blog

English · Français · Deutsch · Español · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어

Table of contents - [💡 What is Univer?](#what-is-univer) - [Open-source capabilities](#open-source-capabilities) - [🚀 Build on the open-source foundation](#what-you-can-build) - [Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor](#quick-start) - [Connect your application to editable content](#connect-your-application-to-editable-content) - [🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture](#open-source-architecture) - [Give custom features clear boundaries](#give-custom-features-clear-boundaries) - [Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo](#compose-cross-feature-edits-and-undoredo) - [Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events](#connect-applications-and-agents-through-facade-apis-and-events) - [🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK](#open-source-and-commercial-extensions) - [Scope and licensing](#scope-and-licensing) - [🌐 Application patterns and ecosystem](#application-patterns-and-ecosystem) - [Univer Workspace: an Office SDK reference application](#univer-workspace-an-office-sdk-reference-application) - [CLI, agent integrations, and developer skills](#cli-agent-integrations-and-developer-skills) - [📚 Documentation and contributing](#documentation-and-contributing) - [Runtime compatibility](#runtime-compatibility) - [💬 Community](#community) - [🔒 Security](#security) - [❤️ Sponsors](#sponsors) - [📄 License](#license)
## 💡 What is Univer?

**Univer** is an Office SDK for building Office applications inside your own product. It provides Office editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing for people and existing agents, using your data and permissions. The product family covers spreadsheets, documents, presentations, relational tables, canvases, and PDFs. Univer Office SDK has three parts: - **Web SDK** is the foundation: content models, editing, rendering, formula calculation, and Facade APIs (application-facing APIs). Compose its plugins into an embedded editor or your own Office application, and reuse the content models, commands, and calculation for Headless processing without an interactive editor. - **Server SDK** adds backend services for real-time collaboration, edit history, and Office file import and export. - **AI SDK** connects Office capabilities to existing agents and workflows, with content tools, execution, and review integrations. **This repository provides the Web SDK's core architecture and engine implementations under Apache-2.0**: content models and snapshot formats, plugin and dependency management, the command system, formula and rendering engines, Facade APIs, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs editing capabilities. Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and commercial AI SDK extensions are distributed and licensed separately. Agents can use the same open-source APIs; your application supplies the model and tool orchestration. The [quotation example](#connect-your-application-to-editable-content) demonstrates editing, calculation, and saving without an AI SDK dependency. ### Open-source capabilities
Area Selected capabilities
Sheets · Editing and layout Cell styles, merged cells, in-cell rich text, freeze panes, floating images, and undo/redo.
Sheets · Data and calculation Formulas, defined names, filtering, sorting, data validation, conditional formatting, hyperlinks, comments, and find and replace.
Docs Rich-text editing, paragraph formatting, lists, hyperlinks, comments, and drawing integration.
Features are composed through plugins and presets; the [quick start](#quick-start) uses only the **Sheets Core preset**. Images use the corresponding drawing plugins. See the [feature comparison](https://univer.ai/compare/) for detailed open-source and commercial coverage. The demos below showcase the wider **Univer Office SDK**, including commercial capabilities. They show more than the default open-source setup; see [open source and commercial extensions](#open-source-and-commercial-extensions) for scope.

## 🚀 Build on the open-source foundation

Your goal Use the open-source foundation Start here
Embed Sheets or Docs Add an editable Office surface to your application or agent product, and connect your data through Facade APIs. Quick start
Process content without an editor Reuse content plugins, models, commands, and calculation in Node.js for editing, snapshots, and automated tasks. Headless guide
Develop custom features or editors Reuse the engines, UI components, plugin boundaries, dependency injection, and command/undo systems. Follow existing features to extend Sheets and Docs or develop your own editors. Open-source architecture
**Coordinate edits and undo/redo across features.** Inserting a row inside a filter range changes both the base content and the filter range; undo needs to restore both. Each feature supplies its own changes and undo data, and the command composes their execution and history. The architecture walkthrough explains how to extend these editing workflows. ### Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor In a browser application using a bundler such as Vite: ```bash pnpm add @univerjs/presets @univerjs/preset-sheets-core ``` Create the container before initializing Univer: ```html
``` ```ts import { UniverSheetsCorePreset } from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core' import UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/locales/en-US' import { createUniver, LocaleType, mergeLocales } from '@univerjs/presets' import '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/lib/index.css' const { univerAPI } = createUniver({ locale: LocaleType.EN_US, locales: { [LocaleType.EN_US]: mergeLocales(UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS), }, presets: [ UniverSheetsCorePreset({ container: 'app', }), ], }) univerAPI.createWorkbook({}) ``` Your page now contains a spreadsheet editor. Use the returned `univerAPI` to work with its content. This example uses open-source packages and needs no commercial Univer license or Server SDK. For component frameworks, retain the `univer` instance returned by `createUniver` and call `univer.dispose()` when the component unmounts. See the [lifecycle guide](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/lifecycle). Presets compose plugins and register their Facade APIs. For manual control, see the [Plugin Mode example](#manual-plugin-composition) below. The [installation guide](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/installation) covers both modes, peer dependencies, and framework integrations. Keep coordinated `@univerjs/*` packages on the same version. Commercial packages must use the matching release line; independently released packages such as icons follow their declared compatibility. See the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md). ### Connect your application to editable content Facade APIs are the application-facing interface to workbooks, worksheets, and ranges. Continue from the quick start to populate a quotation, update a quantity from application code, and read the recalculated total: ```ts // Wait for formula controllers before editing a newly created workbook. await new Promise((resolve) => { if (univerAPI.getCurrentLifecycleStage() >= univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) { resolve() return } const listener = univerAPI.addEvent(univerAPI.Event.LifeCycleChanged, ({ stage }) => { if (stage === univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) { listener.dispose() resolve() } }) }) const workbook = univerAPI.getActiveWorkbook()! const sheet = workbook.getActiveSheet() sheet.getRange('A1:D4').setValues([ ['Item', 'Quantity', 'Unit price', 'Amount'], ['Seats', 2, 25, '=B2*C2'], ['Support', 1, 100, '=B3*C3'], ['Total', '', '', '=SUM(D2:D3)'], ]) // An application control or agent can make the same edit. sheet.getRange('B2').setValue(4) univerAPI.getFormula().onCalculationResultApplied().then(() => { console.log(sheet.getRange('D4').getValue()) // 200 localStorage.setItem('quotation', JSON.stringify(workbook.save())) }).catch(console.error) ``` The editor and your application operate on the same workbook; formula changes are recalculated automatically. `workbook.save()` returns a JSON snapshot containing the workbook and its registered plugin data. Your application owns persistence; this example uses browser storage. On a later page load, after initialization, restore the snapshot **instead of creating a blank workbook**: ```ts const saved = localStorage.getItem('quotation') if (saved) { univerAPI.createWorkbook(JSON.parse(saved)) } ``` This workflow uses only open-source packages. Snapshot persistence is separate from XLSX import and export, which uses the separately distributed file-conversion capabilities. Use public Facade APIs for application integration; the source links below explain internal implementation and extension points. See the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md) before depending on an extension point.
Advanced: compose plugins manually (Plugin Mode) Use Plugin Mode when you need precise control over plugin selection, dependencies, or loading. The preset above handles this composition for you. This alternative initialization uses the same `app` container and the Sheets Core preset's browser plugin stack without a Worker. Use it **instead of** the preset initialization, then run the same quotation example with the returned `univerAPI`. ```bash pnpm add @univerjs/core @univerjs/design @univerjs/docs @univerjs/docs-ui \ @univerjs/engine-formula @univerjs/engine-render @univerjs/network \ @univerjs/sheets @univerjs/sheets-ui @univerjs/sheets-formula \ @univerjs/sheets-formula-ui @univerjs/sheets-numfmt \ spreadsheet rich-text editing. When adding a feature, include its corresponding Facade extensions, locale bundles, and UI styles. Dispose `univer` when its container is unmounted.

## 🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture

### Give custom features clear boundaries Univer organizes content logic and UI interaction in separate plugins. Feature plugins manage rules and content changes; UI plugins provide the interface and user interactions. For example, `sheets-filter` manages filter ranges and rules, while `sheets-filter-ui` provides panels, menus, and shortcuts. ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% A layered overview, not a complete dependency graph. %% Group arrows indicate reuse of the layer below; internal arrows show selected dependencies. flowchart TD subgraph FEATURES["Feature Plugins"] direction LR FUI["Filter
UI Plugin"] VUI["Data Validation
UI Plugin"] FILTER["Filter Plugin"] VALIDATION["Data Validation Plugin"] FUI --> FILTER VUI --> VALIDATION end subgraph PRODUCTS["Product Plugins"] direction LR SUI["Sheets UI Plugin"] SHEETS["Sheets Plugin"] SUI --> SHEETS end subgraph FOUNDATION["Core Framework & Plugins"] direction LR UI["UI Plugin"] FORMULA["Formula Engine Plugin"] RENDER["Render Engine Plugin"] CORE["Core"] UI --> RENDER RENDER --> CORE FORMULA --> CORE end FEATURES --> PRODUCTS PRODUCTS --> FOUNDATION classDef logic fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef ui fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px classDef shared fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef feature fill:#172d50,color:#ffffff,stroke:#172d50 class FUI,VUI ui class FILTER,VALIDATION logic class SUI,SHEETS logic class UI,FORMULA,RENDER,CORE shared style FEATURES fill:#f7fcf9,stroke:#b5d8c1,color:#17543a style PRODUCTS fill:#f5f9ff,stroke:#b6cbea,color:#17365f style FOUNDATION fill:#fafbfc,stroke:#cbd2dc,color:#334155 ``` **Figure 1: three plugin layers.** Feature plugins build on product plugins, which reuse the core framework and plugins. Group arrows show dependencies on the layer below; Core provides content models, commands, dependency injection, and lifecycle management. Some plugins and dependencies are omitted. New features keep their rules in their own plugins and cooperate through public services, commands, and defined extension points. UI plugins build on shared UI services and components. Dependencies are explicit at two levels: - **Between plugins:** `DependentOn` declares runtime plugin dependencies. The plugin service orders them, and lifecycle stages separate dependency registration, content initialization, and UI initialization. - **Inside plugins:** dependency injection connects controllers and services through declared dependencies. Supported overrides let an application replace an implementation, adapt a platform service, or supply a test double. Instance-scoped injectors keep application state separate between Univer instances. Disposable registration also gives commands, listeners, components, and icons a cleanup path when their owner is disposed. The [filter plugin](./packages/sheets-filter/src/plugin.ts) and its [UI plugin](./packages/sheets-filter-ui/src/plugin.ts) show these boundaries in working code.
Inside a feature: Model, Controller, Service, and the UI foundation For filtering, `sheets-filter` owns content logic and `sheets-filter-ui` owns UI interaction. Each module has a focused responsibility. ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% Every arrow means contains. This is code organization, not execution order. flowchart LR FEATURE["Filter Feature"] LOGIC["Filter Plugin"] UI["Filter UI Plugin"] MODEL["Model"] SERVICE["Service"] CONTROLLER["Controller"] COMMAND["Command / Mutation"] FACADE["Facade API"] VIEW["View"] UICTRL["UI Controller"] UISERVICE["UI Service"] FEATURE --> LOGIC FEATURE --> UI LOGIC --> MODEL LOGIC --> SERVICE LOGIC --> CONTROLLER LOGIC --> COMMAND LOGIC --> FACADE UI --> VIEW UI --> UICTRL UI --> UISERVICE classDef logic fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef ui fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px classDef shared fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef feature fill:#172d50,color:#ffffff,stroke:#172d50 class FEATURE feature class LOGIC,MODEL,SERVICE,CONTROLLER,COMMAND,FACADE logic class UI,VIEW,UICTRL,UISERVICE ui ``` **Figure 2: code organization. Arrows mean “contains.”** Both plugins can contain Controllers and Services: logic Controllers coordinate content changes and related features; UI Controllers connect menus, shortcuts, and interactions, with UI Services managing panel state. These responsibilities give new features a consistent structure to implement and test. The UI foundation follows the same division. **`@univerjs/design`** supplies shared components and styles, **`@univerjs/ui`** provides workbench services such as menus, shortcuts, panels, and component registration, and **`@univerjs/icons`** supplies icons. A feature registers its components and icons, contributes menus, and attaches its rendering through these extension points. Teams can add a panel or toolbar feature while reusing the application's UI infrastructure. See the [UI overview](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/ui/overview) and the filter plugin's [component and icon registration](./packages/sheets-filter-ui/src/controllers/components.controller.ts).
### Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo For example, when rows are inserted inside a filter range, the filter plugin supplies the corresponding range change and its undo data. The row command composes the base edit and participating feature changes, executes them, and records their undo/redo information together. The row insertion feature can use the shared extension mechanism while the filter plugin owns its range-update rules. The command system distinguishes three kinds of action: - **Command** orchestrates a business action and the changes it requires. - **Mutation** changes content saved in a snapshot, with serializable parameters. - **Operation** changes transient state, such as an open panel or the scroll position. **A shared structure for undo/redo.** For an undoable edit, the feature implementation supplies the forward mutations and corresponding inverse mutations, and the Command records them through `IUndoRedoService`. When one action affects several features, the Command can combine their changes and undo data in a single undo/redo record, so the user can undo and redo the complete action. See [extending commands](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/custom-command). Features still need to cooperate. **Interceptors and reference-range handlers give that cooperation a defined place.** At supported extension points, plugins contribute checks or related mutations; interceptor priorities control ordering where the API defines it.
Example: commands, callbacks, feature coordination, and undo/redo ```mermaid %%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%% %% Simplified insert-row example. Filter range changes"] MODEL["Execute combined mutations"] UNDO["Record undo and redo"] AFTER["After execution
Notify listeners"] BEFORE --> CMD CMD --> BASE CMD --> EXT BASE --> MODEL EXT --> MODEL MODEL --> UNDO UNDO --> AFTER classDef entry fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px classDef core fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px classDef extension fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px class BEFORE,AFTER entry class CMD,BASE,MODEL,UNDO core class EXT extension ``` This diagram simplifies an insert-row workflow. Nested command executions have their own callbacks; it does not show every event or the separate Operation path. See the [row command](./packages/sheets/src/commands/commands/insert-row-col.command.ts), [filter controller](./packages/sheets-filter/src/controllers/sheets-filter.controller.ts), and [interceptor service](./packages/sheets/src/services/sheet-interceptor/sheet-interceptor.service.ts).
These boundaries support a practical testing strategy: test models and services independently, replace external dependencies through DI, and add regression cases for combined actions and undo/redo. The [filter controller tests](./packages/sheets-filter/src/controllers/__tests__/sheets-filter.controller.spec.ts) exercise row and column changes and their effect on filtering. ### Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events The repository includes the content models, formula engine, and Canvas rendering and layout engine behind the editors. They are shared building blocks: spreadsheet rich text, for example, reuses document layout and rendering. Custom features can build on these engines instead of implementing a separate content stack. Read about the [formula engine architecture](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/formula) and [rendering engine architecture](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/rendering). Browser editors, Node.js Headless tasks, and appropriately composed Workers can reuse the corresponding content plugins, models, commands, and calculation. See [Headless Univer](https://docs.univer.ai/guides/sheets/getting-started/node) and the [isomorphic architecture](./docs/ISOMORPHIC.md). `ICommandService` exposes execution callbacks so plugins can observe commands before and after execution. Facade APIs wrap the underlying capabilities in application objects such as `FWorkbook`, `FWorksheet`, and `FRange`. Each plugin contributes its own Facade extensions, **typed events through `univerAPI.Event`**, and **enums through `univerAPI.Enum`**. Application code can discover event names and constants from one entry point instead of importing private services or repeating strings. For example, `BeforeCommandExecute` can inspect and cancel an execution; `CommandExecuted` reports executions to listeners. Listeners return disposables, and cancellation applies where the event supports it. Facade extensions stay with their feature packages, so a content API does not have to pull in unrelated UI APIs. See the [Facade design](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/facade), [command callbacks and event bridge](./packages/core/src/facade/f-univer.ts), and [Enum entry point](./packages/core/src/facade/f-enum.ts). The repository provides working feature implementations and patterns for extending them. Read the [filter implementation walkthrough](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/anatomy) for a complete example, or the [API Stability Policy](./docs/API_STABILITY.md) before depending on an extension point.

## 🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK

When you want more ready-to-integrate capabilities, compose the corresponding **Univer Office SDK** modules: additional content types, advanced editing plugins, collaboration, file conversion, and agent tooling. They extend the same content models, plugin architecture, command system, and Facade design introduced above, so you can build on your existing integration.
Part How it extends the foundation
Open-source Web SDK core · this repository Open-source models, engines, plugins, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs capabilities, with corresponding Headless content operations. Use them in commercial applications under Apache-2.0.
Commercial Web SDK plugins Follow the core's Plugin, dependency injection, Command/Mutation, and Facade extension patterns. Add charts, shapes, pivot tables, SmartArt, and other features for the corresponding content types.
Server SDK Extends the same content models and mutation conventions with real-time collaboration, revision history, and Office file conversion. Integrates with your application's identity, permissions, and storage.
AI SDK extensions Reuse Web SDK Headless and Facade capabilities to provide composable Node.js APIs and CLI building blocks for agents to inspect, edit, and check content, with collaboration and Worktree review integrations.
### Scope and licensing - **This repository:** Apache-2.0 packages that can be used in commercial applications under that license, including the open-source Headless content capabilities. - **Commercial extensions:** Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and AI SDK capabilities beyond the open-source foundation are distributed and licensed separately. **Freemium** evaluation includes watermarks and feature limits. - **Reference applications:** Open-source applications such as Univer Workspace have their own source licenses. Their SDK dependencies retain their respective licenses. See the [feature comparison](https://univer.ai/compare/), including its **Open source only** filter, for detailed coverage and [plans and licensing](https://univer.ai/pricing/) for commercial options.
How shared content models connect editing, collaboration, and files These capabilities operate on serializable **Unit snapshots**, including Sheets' `IWorkbookData`, Docs' `IDocumentData`, Slides' `ISlideData`, and canvases' `IBoardData` (called **Boards** in the API). These types come from core and the respective product packages; current Slides and Boards capabilities are separately distributed commercial products. The shared Unit conventions let browser editors, backend services, and agents work with the same content. Commands orchestrate edits; **Mutations describe content changes**. Collaboration packages those mutations into **changesets**, applies **operational transformation (OT)** to concurrent changes, and manages confirmed revisions and snapshots. History can reconstruct a revision from a snapshot and subsequent changesets. Read the [collaboration design](https://docs.univer.ai/blog/ot) and [Collaboration SDK overview](https://docs.univer.ai/server/collaboration/overview). **Exchange** maps Office file structures to and from Univer content snapshots. For OOXML formats such as **XLSX, DOCX, and PPTX**, it parses the file into the corresponding Sheet, Doc, or Slide data and generates the file representation on export. The converted content can enter the same editing, calculation, collaboration, and agent workflows. See [Office file import and export](https://docs.univer.ai/server/import-export/node).
How AI SDK gives agents the same content capabilities AI SDK builds on the Web SDK's **Headless content models, commands, calculation, and Facade APIs**. It exposes structured TypeScript APIs and optional Commander presets that applications can compose into their own Office CLI or agent tools. - **Understand, discover, and edit.** Inspection returns structured content. API Reference helps the agent find Facade symbols and signatures shipped with its SDK. Facade execution distinguishes read and write modes, captures mutations, and works with explicit synchronization and commit results. See [content operations](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/content-operations). - **Check the rendered result.** A browser Render Runtime reuses Web SDK rendering for screenshots. Slide layout lint adds structured findings for issues such as off-page or overlapping text, giving the agent evidence for another editing pass. See [visual inspection](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/visual-inspection). - **Edit drafts for human review.** With the corresponding collaboration and Web capabilities, agents can edit and verify an isolated Worktree draft over several rounds, then hand it to a person to review, merge, or reopen. The workflow uses the same snapshots, mutations, and revision conventions. See [Worktree](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/worktree). For repeated calls, optional [Worker pools and a daemon](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/runtime-architecture) reuse loaded content instances and reduce repeated initialization. Your application owns the root CLI, targets, authorization, and output. Explore the [AI SDK package catalog](https://docs.univer.ai/ai/packages) to select the required capabilities.

"Tailscale without Tailscale, by Tailscale"

# Tailcat Tailcat is a remix of Tailscale open source pieces to act like [netcat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netcat), but over Tailscale's data plane, without Tailscale's control plane. Tailscale's data plane (`magicsock`, internally) gives you point-to-point WireGuard®-encrypted tunnels between two machines with DERP as the NAT-hole-punching communication side channel and the ultimate relay-of-last-resort if NAT traversal fails. Instead of using the Tailscale control plane, all `tailcat` connection metadata is exchanged out of band, however you want. The `tailcat` CLI (in `cmd/tailcat`) is built on the `tailcat` Go library (importable as [`github.com/tailscale/tailcat`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/tailscale/tailcat)). Whether you use `tailcat` as a CLI tool or library, one side runs a `tailcat` server (listener) and gets back a short tailcat address. The other side passes that tailcat address to `tailcat`'s client side to connect. All traffic between the two is encrypted end-to-end with WireGuard. The initial connection bootstraps through a DERP server ([see below](#bring-your-own-derp-relay)), and then magicsock performs NAT traversal to upgrade to a direct peer-to-peer UDP connection when possible (usually!). You don't need a Tailscale account, root/admin access on the machine (it doesn't alter your machine's routing tables, DNS, etc.). It's just a userspace library and CLI tool. And it's all open source. You can use our free rate-limited DERP relays (the default DERP map is https://tailcat.dev/derpmap.json) or you can [run your own](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/tree/main/cmd/derper#derp). There's also an experimental in-browser web demo (tailcat compiled to WebAssembly) at https://tailscale.github.io/tailcat/ that can send and receive files or text, interoperating with the CLI. Browser traffic is relayed over DERP only, with no direct connections until WebRTC support ([#4](https://github.com/tailscale/tailcat/issues/4)). ## Install See [INSTALL.md](./INSTALL.md) for details on each, including notes for packagers building from source: | Method | Linux | macOS | Windows | FreeBSD,
